name: who-owns-loop
title: Who Owns the Loop?
kicker: AI in the loop · not a person rubber-stamping a machine
html:
Who Owns the Loop?

The Person Owns the Goal

Said in a sentence. Read back as a kept script.

The Model Supports

Finds the way once. Repairs when the controls change.

The Controls Hold the Line

Hooks for the builder, the server’s forms for the agent. I read the record, not every step.
say: You may have heard 'human in the loop' used as a comfort blanket: put a person at the end of the pipeline to approve whatever the machine decided. Ask that person to approve five hundred decisions a day and see how much reviewing actually happens. Probably not much. There's a better framing, and it isn't mine. Sriraam Natarajan, Kristian Kersting and their co-authors call it AI in the loop: the human is in control of the system, and the AI is there to support the human. Stanford HAI put it plainly in 2022: control should remain in human hands. And Ben Shneiderman showed years ago that more automation doesn't have to mean less control; well-designed systems offer high levels of both. Notice how that maps onto what I described a minute ago. I own the goal; I say it in a sentence. The model finds the way once, and what it found is kept as a script I can read. The hooks and the server's own controls hold the line while I'm walking the dog. I don't approve every step; I read the record. That's high automation and high control at the same time, and it's the arrangement this talk asks for, for agents calling APIs too.

deck:ref.name: ai-in-the-loop
deck:ref.label: AI-IN-THE-LOOP
deck:ref.title: AI in the loop: the person in control, the AI in support
deck:ref.summary: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting contrast human-in-the-loop systems with AI-in-the-loop (AI²L) systems, where the human is in control of the system and the AI is there to support the human, and argue that evaluations should not judge the machine component alone.
deck:ref.quote: “We argue that existing evaluation methods often overemphasize the machine (learning) component's performance, neglecting the human expert's critical role.”
deck:ref.cite: Natarajan, Mathur, Sidheekh, Stammer and Kersting, “Human-in-the-loop or AI-in-the-loop? Automate or Collaborate?”, arXiv

deck:ref.title: High automation and high human control, together
deck:ref.summary: Shneiderman's human-centered AI framework: more automation does not have to mean less human control. Well-designed systems offer both.
deck:ref.quote: “Well-designed technologies that offer high levels of human control and high levels of computer automation can increase human performance, leading to wider adoption.”

deck:ref.label: REASON
deck:ref.title: Reason: the part everyone's excited about
deck:ref.summary: Reasoning models can stand in for a person in two places: finding the way the first time, and repairing when the controls change. Everywhere else, paying a model to reason through the same path again is the token maxing Hightower warned about. Useful at the edges; wasted in the middle.
